chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Muawiya ibn Maysara, from al-Hakam ibn Uteyba, who said:

I saw Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and he had taken henna and applied it to his nails, so he said: 'O Hakam, what do you say about this?' I said: 'What could I say when you are doing it, and indeed among us the young men do it.' He said: 'O Hakam, indeed when the nails are affected by the henna (noura), it changes them until they resemble the nails of the dead, so change them with henna.'

key_terms.أَظَافِيرَ الْمَوْتَى: Nails of the dead, implying a darker, duller color
key_terms.النُّورَةُ: Pure henna or the staining effect of henna, often referring to the reddish-brown dye
key_terms.الْحِنَّاء: Henna (lawsonia inermis), used here for dyeing and beautification

ai.seo_question: Why did Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) recommend applying henna to nails after using pure henna?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that the darkening of nails by *noura* (pure henna) can resemble the appearance of the deceased, prompting the recommendation to apply henna again to restore a vibrant, living appearance. This reflects the Shia emphasis on *tazkiyah* (purification) and *takhalluq* (adornment with good character/appearance) as acts of worship that enhance one's dignity and readiness for prayer. The practice underscores the balance between ritual purity and aesthetic care in daily Islamic life.
